001: Something unsafe is happening now (burning smell, smoke, sparks, gas smell, an alarm, water or ice at electrical parts, or someone at risk)
002: Stop checking. We’ll show you where to get help.
005: Look from where you’re standing or from a window. Don’t open, touch, climb on, or reach into the unit.
006: Don’t put hands, sticks, or tools through the grille or into the fins, even with the power off. Parts inside the outdoor unit can stay charged after the power is off, and wind turning the fan can charge them again.
007: Don’t try to stop, turn, or free the fan, even with the system off.
008: Answer from where you’re standing or from a window. Don’t open or touch anything to find out.
009: Answer from a few steps back. Don’t touch the unit, the disconnect box on the wall, or the wiring.
010: Before we look at the outdoor unit: is the house getting too cold for anyone in it? If anyone at home is a baby, an older adult, or has a medical need, or the indoor temperature keeps dropping, getting them warm comes first.
011: Get everyone warm first. If someone is confused, very drowsy, or hard to wake, call 911. Then call a licensed HVAC professional and tell them the house is cold.
012: Stop. Running an iced-up outdoor unit can damage it. If your thermostat doesn’t have an Emergency Heat setting, turn the system Off at the thermostat. Let the ice melt on its own. Don’t chip ice, pour hot water on it, or try to speed up the defrost. If the house is getting cold, call a licensed HVAC professional. If it’s dangerously cold and anyone is at risk, get them somewhere warm first.
013: Stop. Turn it off and let the ice melt. Ice on the outdoor unit while cooling isn’t normal. Turn the system Off at the thermostat and leave it off until all the ice is gone. Don’t chip ice or pour hot water on it. Then call a licensed HVAC professional.
014: This is a job for a technician. The inside of this unit can stay electrically charged after the power is off, and wind turning the fan can charge it again. Don’t remove panels or covers, and don’t press buttons on the board inside. Codes are read from your thermostat, remote, wall control, or app.
015: Anything inside the grille or deep in the fins is for a technician to clear.
016: Refrigerant work needs an EPA-certified technician. If you hear hissing, turn the system Off at the thermostat. Don’t touch the pipes, valves, or caps.
017: Don’t use a ladder, chair, or stool, go on a roof, or walk on ice to reach the unit. Look from a window or from dry, level ground in daylight, or let a professional check it.
018: This guide doesn’t cover resetting breakers or turning the disconnect back on. You can look, but don’t switch anything. If a breaker looks tripped or the disconnect is off, leave it as it is and call a licensed HVAC professional or electrician. It may have been turned off on purpose, or because of a problem a pro should find. A breaker that trips again is a warning sign. Don’t reset it.
019: Stop. Keep everyone clear of the unit. Don’t push, prop, or try to level it. If you can get to the thermostat indoors without going near the unit, turn the system Off. Call your installer or an HVAC professional today.
020: Someone at home is getting too cold (a baby, an older adult, or someone with a medical need)
021: In cold weather, a cloud of steam from the outdoor unit during defrost can be normal. If you’re not sure it’s steam, or you smell burning, treat it as smoke.
023: Write the code down exactly as it’s shown, or take a photo of it. For a blinking light, count the blinks for a full minute. A short phone video helps.
024: Don’t clear the code, delete the error history, reset the unit, or switch the power off and on to make the code go away. The code and its history help your technician.
025: The display on the board inside the outdoor unit is for technicians. Reaching it means removing panels.
026: These code meanings come from manufacturers’ documents for some models. Your model may differ. A code explains what the unit detected. It isn’t a diagnosis.
027: You’ve written down the code. Tell your technician the code, how it was shown, and what you saw. Don’t clear or reset it before the visit.
028: The manufacturer describes this code as normal operation or as running in a limited range. If heating or cooling has stopped, or the house is getting uncomfortable, call a licensed HVAC professional now. If not, tell your technician about it.
029: These numbers are only for the models named. Your unit’s installation manual lists its own numbers. Check your unit’s manual. They describe how the unit should be installed. They aren’t a check of your unit.
030: Look from cleared ground or a window. Don’t walk on ice or climb snowbanks to get closer.
031: Don’t use a shovel, plow, or snowblower near the unit or pile snow against it, and don’t chip ice off it.
032: Defrost water is refreezing on the path. Treat the path the way you normally would, but keep salt and ice melt off the unit. Ask your installer about sending the water somewhere it won’t freeze on a path.
033: Don’t push, lean on, or try to level the unit.
034: If the outdoor unit hums but the fan won’t turn, turn the system Off at the thermostat and leave it off until a professional checks it.
035: A fan that scrapes or grinds can break. Turn the system Off at the thermostat and leave it off until a professional checks it.
036: Don’t go outside in the dark, in a storm, or on ice to check. Describe what you can see to a professional, or check again in daylight when the ground is clear.
037: Hot or greasy air blowing at the outdoor unit makes it work harder. Keep grills and portable heaters away from it, and tell your installer about any vent aimed at it.
038: Stored items, covers, and plants close to the unit can make it breathe its own exhaust. Keep them clear of the unit, but don’t reach into, cover, or move the unit itself.
039: The house is getting cold. Call a licensed HVAC professional now and tell them so.
040: From what you saw, that sounds like a normal defrost. If the ice comes back and stays, the unit stops clearing, or the house gets cold, call a licensed HVAC professional.
041: Nothing you could see outside the unit explains the problem. A professional needs to test the system.
042: Test session: these answers were made up for practice. This isn’t a record of real equipment.
043: Homeowner-reported answers only. Not confirmed by a technician, and not an inspection.
044: Don’t change these. They protect your equipment and your safety, and they’re for professionals only: any side, top, or front panel or cover; the electrical or control box; the disconnect box and its handle or fuses; buttons, switches, or displays on the board inside the unit; the fan blade and fan motor; refrigerant valves, caps, and pipes; the pipe cover and insulation; the stand, wall bracket, and their bolts; any heater, sensor, or wire on the unit; service menus and anything that clears or deletes stored codes or error history. If a step would take you to one of these, stop. If a screen asks you to enter a password or access code, stop. That’s for installers. Writing down an error code that’s already showing is fine.
045: The fan on this kind of unit blows air out sideways. Some of the checks are different, so we’ll use the checks made for it.
046: If you’re not sure whether it’s steam or smoke, choose the hazard option.
047: If a code is already showing on the thermostat, remote, wall control, or app, write it down or take a photo. Don’t open the outdoor unit to look for a code, and don’t open service menus or clear codes.
048: The unit is tipping, falling, or pulling away from the wall
049: Hissing at the pipe connections (not the whoosh during a defrost), or fresh oily spots at the pipes or valves
050: For example, Carrier lists at least 24 in. in front of the fan for its 38MURA models (IM-38MURA-02, p. 8). Daikin lists a wall on the fan side as no taller than 47 in. for its Fit models (3P515859-5S, p. 4). Check your unit’s manual.
051: For example, Carrier lists at least 2 in. above the deepest expected snow for its 38MURA models (IM-38MURA-02, p. 8). Daikin lists the bottom frame at more than 19-3/4 in. above expected snowfall for its Fit models (3P515859-5S, p. 6). Check your unit’s manual.
052: Never heat with an oven, stove, grill, or generator indoors (carbon monoxide). If you use an electric space heater, plug it straight into a wall outlet, follow its maker’s instructions, and keep it clear of anything that can burn.
053: You’ve cleared around the outside of the unit and set the thermostat back. If it still isn’t heating or cooling the way it should after it’s run for a while, or the same problem comes back, call a licensed HVAC professional.
054: You’ve cleared the snow around the unit and set the thermostat back. After more snow, check again from cleared ground in daylight. If ice builds up on the unit, it keeps getting buried, or it still isn’t heating the way it should, call a licensed HVAC professional.
055: Outside, a cloud of steam can rise from the outdoor unit while it defrosts, and that can be normal. Ice that stays on the outdoor unit and keeps building isn’t a normal defrost. Look from a step back, and don’t touch the unit.
056: Don’t try to speed it up, and don’t chip, pry, or pour water on the ice.
057: If the code means the unit is defrosting (for example, DF on some Carrier models):
058: The heat pump check covers thermostat settings that keep the outdoor unit off on purpose. If you haven’t done that check, start a new check and choose the heat pump option.
060: From the thermostat, wall control, remote, or app only — don’t open the unit.
062: There isn’t enough to go on. Describe what you saw to a licensed HVAC professional.
063: Not normal: a solid block of ice that keeps growing, or a grille iced shut.
101: What this does: Keeps stored items, covers, and plants away from the outside of the unit so it can breathe. Caution: The fins bend easily, and the fan can start on its own at any time.
102: 1. Write down how the thermostat is set, then turn the system Off at the thermostat. This doesn’t cut power to the unit, so stay outside the grilles. 2. Move planters, toys, covers, and stored items away from the unit. 3. Trim plants back by hand or with hand pruners, keeping the pruners and clippings away from the unit. 4. Pick up loose leaves and clippings from the ground around the unit. Don’t touch the coil or fins at all, by hand or with any tool. Don’t reach through the grille, use a pressure washer, or spray water near the electrical side. Leave anything on the fins, stuck in them, or behind the grille for a professional. 5. Put the thermostat back the way you wrote it down.
103: Stop and put the thermostat back the way you wrote it down if anything near the electrical box is wet or icy, if you’d have to reach inside the grille, or if the fan starts while you’re close. If that doesn’t fix it, call a licensed HVAC professional.
104: What this does: Moves loose snow away from the unit so it can breathe and defrost water can drain. Caution: Snow and ice around the unit are slippery, and the fins bend easily.
105: 1. Only go out if you can stand on cleared, level ground in daylight. Don’t use a ladder or climb a snowbank. 2. Write down how the thermostat is set, then turn the system Off at the thermostat. 3. Clear loose snow from the ground around the unit and in front of the fan, by hand or with a soft broom, so air can move and defrost water can drain. Don’t clear snow off the coil or fins, and don’t touch them at all, by hand or with any tool. They bend easily. 4. Don’t use a shovel or snowblower near the unit, and don’t pile snow against it. 5. Leave ice alone: don’t chip, pry, or hit it, and don’t use hot water, a heat gun, or a torch. 6. Put the thermostat back the way you wrote it down.
106: Stop if snow or ice is packed against the electrical box or disconnect, if there’s ice inside the grille, or if the footing is icy, and call a licensed HVAC professional. If ice is building up on the coil or the unit is encased in ice, leave the system Off at the thermostat, don’t chip the ice, and call a licensed HVAC professional.
108: After you set the thermostat back, watch from a few steps back for about 10 minutes.
109: After you set the thermostat back, watch from inside for up to 15 minutes. A cloud of steam and a stopped outdoor fan can be part of a normal defrost.
